text: Background: I work for OpenAI as an AI safety researcher, doing research on constrained RL and safe exploration. I don't work on OpenAI comms, but I've collaborated closely with them for a few releases (Spinning Up, Safety Gym). I respect their work and value them as colleagues.

author: jachiam0
text: AI research Twitter: what concrete norms/checklists do you think research orgs should use to communicate about AI science to mixed audiences that include some AI researchers but also lots of other people (many nontechnical)?

author: jachiam0
text: @nimish15shah @zacharylipton @catherineols @ilyasut @OpenAI What are your thoughts on the best way to do citations and credit sharing in a blog post meant for a mixed audience of AI researchers and non-scientists?

author: jachiam0
text: @nimish15shah @zacharylipton @catherineols @ilyasut @OpenAI It seems fair to argue that in-line hyperlinks are an insufficient form of academic credit attribution, and something else should be done. I'm happy to engage productively on this! But I don't think there's a fair argument that the blog post was written in bad faith.

author: jachiam0
text: @nimish15shah @zacharylipton @catherineols @ilyasut @OpenAI The immediate next words are "the double descent phenomenon," where each of "double," "descent," and "phenomenon" is a hyperlink to a prior work that contributed to establishing the phenomenon.

text: @catherineols @zacharylipton @ilyasut @OpenAI Happy to discuss offline, not sure unpacking root causes of complex value judgments fits in Tweets.

"Well-established" to you is new to many, including some ML academics and many more ML non-academics. (3) The eighth word of the blog links to past work.

text: @catherineols @zacharylipton @ilyasut @OpenAI I think it expects a lot out of a Tweet to simultaneously do an effective job communicating an idea, and be a complete work of scholarship. I think it's a very reasonable middle ground to share an idea as a lede to a work of scholarship. (3/n)

text: @catherineols @zacharylipton @ilyasut @OpenAI In something like a Tweet, where your space is constricted to a ridiculous degree, you should try to communicate whatever idea is actually most valuable to the audience for the audience. (2/n)

author: jachiam0
text: @catherineols @zacharylipton @ilyasut @OpenAI I think I would reject the premise of the question, because it depends deeply on the communications medium and the audience. For standard academic communications like talks or papers, you have the opportunity to cover everything because of time and space alotted. (1/n)

author: jachiam0
text: @catherineols @zacharylipton @ilyasut @OpenAI Two thoughts: 1) It isn't as informative about the phenomenon (does not describe the up-down-up, which is the interesting thing), and 2) my prior is to feel skeptical that it would be received very differently.

author: jachiam0
text: @zacharylipton @catherineols @ilyasut @OpenAI I respectfully disagree. The tweet doesn't say something like "we've found" or "we've discovered" or anything of the form to indicate that it's a new phenomenon discovered only by OpenAI. It just states an empirically-observed fact and links to an informational blog post.

text: With Safety Gym, we make a step forward by providing a bunch of fun constrained RL environments, and discuss what to measure and why. (Paper: https://t.co/j0mVh1Hs1W, Envs: https://t.co/4AkTZ5hNgb)

author: jachiam0
text: Main ideas: constraints are a natural way to embed safety into RL agents, so we would like to be able to do research on constrained RL easily. But it's been hard to do, because it's been hard to measure progress: few environments for constrained RL, no easy-to-compare metrics.

author: jachiam0
text: Super excited to ship this resource for doing research on safe reinforcement learning, in collaboration with Alex Ray and Dario Amodei!

quoted.text:
We're releasing Safety Gym, environments and tools to evaluate reinforcement learning with safety constraints: https://t.co/3fj0at6UVV

Aims to ultimately help agents satisfy real-world safety requirements while training (eg not driving off a cliff, not writing abusive content). https://t.co/VTwS4KoFS1
